# ThreadSanitizer suppression list - KEPT NARROW, AND EVERY LINE IS MEASURED.
#
# Run 36063084319 (commit 444f938) was the first time the ThreadSanitizer job
# ran to completion. What it measured:
#
#   test result: ok. 3220 passed; 0 failed   (4270.64 s)
#   WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race       x 354
#
# Every one of those 354 reports has `sled 0.34.7` somewhere in its stack;
# not a single report is free of it. The split:
#
#   306  free -> std::sys::alloc::unix::dealloc   (dropping sled objects)
#    48  <sled::pagecache::segment::SegmentAccountant as Drop>::drop
#         (sled-0.34.7/src/pagecache/segment.rs:140)
#
# So the races are not in our concurrency code; they are on the dependency's
# shutdown path: sled leaves its background threads unjoined at close and the
# same memory is touched from both sides while dropping. sled 0.34.7 is the
# last release of that crate and it is unmaintained.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT A `race:` RULE ACTUALLY MATCHES, AND WHY THREE RULES WERE DELETED
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# A `race:` rule is a substring test run against EVERY frame of BOTH stacks in
# a report - the reporting access and the previous one. It is not a filter on
# "races inside sled". It is a filter on "reports that touch sled anywhere".
#
# That distinction is the whole risk, and it was raised as a review finding on
# PR #81: the storage layer is `sled::Db`, threaded through the node's state
# handling, so a genuine race in OUR code whose other access merely passes
# through a sled entry point would match a module-wide rule and be silenced.
# The job would stay green with a real race hidden inside the `matched` count.
#
# The finding is correct about the mechanism, so the list is now cut along the
# line that separates the two cases:
#
#   DELETED - these name sled's PUBLIC API, which is exactly where our own
#   code stands when it calls into the store, so a rule here can cover an
#   application race:
#
#       race:sled::tree        `Tree::insert/get/update_and_fetch/...`
#       race:sled::Db          the handle held by src/storage/db.rs
#       race:sled::context     opened and dropped through the public handle
#
#   KEPT - these name sled's internal machinery. Our code holds no reference
#   into them, never calls them, and cannot be on the racing side of an access
#   whose only sled frames are these:
#
#       race:sled::pagecache   the 48 SegmentAccountant::drop reports above
#       race:sled::arc         sled's own refcount container, dropped at close
#       race:sled::ivec        sled's own buffer type, dropped at close
#
# Not measured yet, and said plainly: whether the three deleted rules were
# carrying any of the 354 reports. They were written from the shape of the
# stacks, not from a per-rule count, because the run that produced the 354 did
# not print one. The job now prints the per-rule table on every run, so the
# next run answers it. If a deleted rule turns out to have been load-bearing
# the reports come back as SURVIVING warnings and the job goes red - which is
# the correct outcome: a rule is re-added with the count that justifies it,
# never because the gate was inconvenient.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT KEEPS THIS LIST FROM BECOMING A BLINDFOLD
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
#   * Two canaries run WITH this list, not without it.
#     - the plain canary: two threads, one address, no sled anywhere. Proves
#       the tool still sees a race at all.
#     - the sled-frame canary: one thread writes the racing address from
#       inside a closure sled calls, the other writes it directly. The report
#       therefore carries `sled::tree::Tree::update_and_fetch` in one of its
#       two stacks while the racing memory is ours. This is precisely the
#       shape the review finding describes. If a rule ever swallows it the
#       canary sees no warning and the job fails. Re-adding `race:sled::tree`
#       would fail this canary on the next run rather than quietly widening
#       the filter.
#   * `print_suppressions=1` is on and the job prints the PER-RULE hit table.
#     A rule that matched nothing is dead weight and the step fails until the
#     line is deleted; the total is compared against the measured baseline and
#     a jump has to be read before it is accepted.
#   * any warning that survives the list is counted, and a non-zero count
#     fails the step.
#
# This file is not the fix. The fix is moving off an unmaintained embedded
# key-value store, which is tracked in issue #80. The list is valid until
# then, and every time it changes the measurement above is taken again.

race:sled::pagecache
race:sled::arc
race:sled::ivec
